title: Word formation at C1
tagline: Turn words into the right part of speech: suffixes, negative prefixes, compounds and Part 3 strategy.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 3 — word formation (the whole task)
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (prefix and suffix collocations)
Writing Parts 1 and 2 — precise, varied vocabulary instead of repeating the same word class
Listening Part 4 — recognising derived words spoken at natural speed
why: Part 3 rewards exactly one skill: seeing past the root word to the part of speech the gap actually needs — noun, adjective, negative adjective, or verb. The same suffixes and prefixes also raise the level of essays and reports, where a nominalisation like disillusionment reads as noticeably more advanced than people don't believe in it any more, and a precise negative prefix shows control that a vague 'not' never can.

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: verb → abstract noun (a quality or state)
noun → a state, period or group
prefix + base = negative, with different nuances
noun/verb used as the other word class, unchanged

use.point: Nominalising suffixes: turning actions and qualities into nouns

examples.text: Her sudden resignation shocked the whole department.
The council questioned the project's long-term viability.
There's a growing sense of disillusionment among young voters.
The witness's account was inconsistent with the evidence.
examples.note: in-, a simple negative before certain roots

examples.text: He misjudged the distance and missed the bus by seconds.

examples.note: non-, formal/technical, a category rather than a fault

use.point: Compound adjectives that pack a description into one word

examples.text: It was a well-established tradition long before Miss Vega arrived.
Filling in the census forms is a genuinely time-consuming job.
The volcano's ash-covered slopes made the climb even harder.
Teachers now google unfamiliar terms in front of the class without embarrassment.
examples.note: conversion: noun used directly as a verb

examples.text: New regulations will strengthen safety checks on school trips.
The ministry wants to modernise the exam system within five years.

watch_out.why: the sentence needs the noun form (resignation), not the bare verb.
mis- (wrongly), not un-, is the prefix that means 'did it incorrectly'.
non- usually keeps a hyphen before the base word, unlike un-/dis-/in-.
compound adjectives before a noun need a hyphen: well-established, not well established.

watch_out.wrong: The council doubted the project's viable.
watch_out.why: after a possessive, the sentence needs the noun (viability), not the adjective viable.

watch_out.wrong: The ministry wants to modern the exam system.
watch_out.right: The ministry wants to modernise the exam system.
watch_out.why: modern is an adjective; the verb needs the -ise suffix, modernise.

dialogue.title: Quick round
dialogue.context: Miss Vega runs a rapid vocabulary round, and the conversation about student council reform turns out to supply most of the examples itself.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Quick round — give me a sentence with a word from today's list.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: The head boy's resignation caught everyone off guard.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Because he completely misjudged how much work the role actually needed.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Or maybe he just wanted to modernise the student council instead.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: There's definitely disillusionment among the younger students about how it's run.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: The whole system feels well-established, if a bit outdated.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Rewriting the constitution would be seriously time-consuming, though.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: True — but I'd rather we strengthen the rules than scrap them completely.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Can I just say I love that 'to google' counts as a real verb now?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: It does. Language changes — a non-negotiable fact of life.

items.sentence: Her sudden ___ shocked the whole department.
items.why: the sentence needs the noun form (resignation) as the subject, not the bare verb or gerund used loosely here.

items.sentence: He completely ___ the distance and missed the bus.
items.why: mis- (wrongly) is the prefix for judging something incorrectly; unjudged and disjudged are not real words.

items.sentence: The clause is legally ___ in every contract we sign.
items.why: non- combines with negotiable in this fixed expression, and normally keeps the hyphen.

items.sentence: It's a ___ tradition at this school.
items.why: before a noun, the compound adjective needs a hyphen: well-established.

items.sentence: The council questioned the plan's long-term ___.
items.why: after 'the plan's long-term', the sentence needs the noun (viability), not the adjective viable.

items.sentence: The ministry wants to ___ the exam system within five years.
items.why: modern is the adjective; the verb form needs the -ise suffix: modernise.

items.sentence: There's growing ___ among young voters about politics.
items.why: disillusionment (dis- + noun) names the state of feeling; illusion and disillusion don't fit as the subject here.

summary: Nominalising suffixes turn a verb or adjective into a noun: -ance/-ence, -ity, -ism, -hood.
Negative prefixes are not interchangeable: un-/in-/dis- = simple opposite, mis- = wrongly, non- = outside the category.
Compound adjectives like well-established and time-consuming keep their hyphen before a noun.
-en, -ify, -ise turn an adjective or noun into a verb; there's no single rule for which suffix a word takes.
In Part 3, read the whole sentence first — the gap needs a specific part of speech, not just 'a version of the word'.
